title: Sequence Models: the RNN/LSTM Baseline
oneLineScope: The recurrent sequence models transformers replaced, and the two problems — vanishing gradients and inherent sequentiality — that doomed them.
prose:
Where we are. Before transformers, this is how neural networks handled sequences — and these are the two problems that motivated everything that came after. If you have been reading this graph in order, you have just seen how word embeddings give each token a position in a continuous vector space. The natural next question is: how does a network actually process a sequence of those vectors? The answer, through most of the 2010s, was the recurrent neural network, extended by the Long Short-Term Memory cell. Understanding what these models do and where they break is the prerequisite for understanding why alignment, attention, and ultimately the transformer were necessary.

The gist. A recurrent net reads a sequence one token at a time, threading a hidden state from step to step that is supposed to carry everything relevant from the past. LSTMs improve on this by adding learned gates that can preserve information across many steps, solving the worst of the gradient problems. But two fundamental difficulties remain. First, gradients still struggle to carry information across very long distances — the vanishing-gradient problem is mitigated, not solved. Second, and more important for scaling, the sequential structure is irreducible: each step must wait for the previous one, so you cannot parallelize across the length of a sequence no matter how many processors you have.

Why it matters. These two problems are the direct ancestors of the transformer’s architecture. Attention fixes the long-range bottleneck by letting every position reach every other position directly, bypassing the sequential chain entirely. The next node, alignment and attention, traces how that fix was first discovered. Arriving at this node with the RNN’s limitations clearly in mind is what makes that story legible.

The basic recurrent network

The core idea is simple enough to state in one sentence: use the same weights at every time step, and feed the previous output back in as an extra input. This is exactly the structure that was explored in the backprop-era PDP program. A plain RNN reads a sequence of tokens (a token is the atomic unit the model operates on — a word, subword piece, or character) left to right, updating a hidden state vector at each step:

\[ h_t = f\!\left(W_x\, x_t + W_h\, h_{t-1} + b\right) \]

Here \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\) is the current input — typically a word embedding, a dense vector representing the token; \(h_t, h_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) are the hidden states at steps \(t\) and \(t{-}1\), each a vector of width \(d_h\); \(W_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_{\text{in}}}\) and \(W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_h}\) are learned weight matrices shared across all steps; \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) is a bias; and \(f\) is a nonlinearity such as \(\tanh\). An output can be read from \(h_t\) at each step, or only at the final step, depending on the task. The weight-sharing is the recurrence — the same \(W_x\) and \(W_h\) appear at every position.

Training uses backpropagation through time (BPTT): unroll the recurrence into a computation graph with \(T\) copies of the same weights, then run ordinary backpropagation on that unrolled graph. If you know backprop, you already know BPTT — the only novelty is that \(W_h\) appears at every step, so its gradient is the sum of contributions from all positions. This is exactly the structure from the PDP literature, just applied to a sequential chain rather than a feedforward stack.

Problem 1 — vanishing and exploding gradients

Imagine tracing a signal that must travel from token 1 to token 50: something early in a sentence that matters for understanding something near the end. The gradient of the loss with respect to an early hidden state \(h_k\) flows back through the chain \(h_T \to h_{T-1} \to \cdots \to h_k\). At each step it is multiplied by the Jacobian of \(f\) with respect to the previous state — roughly a factor of \(\|W_h\|\) combined with the derivative of \(f\). Across \(T - k\) steps, that factor is raised to the \((T{-}k)\)-th power. If the dominant singular value of the relevant Jacobian is less than one, the gradient shrinks exponentially toward zero; if it exceeds one, it explodes. Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi (1994) gave the precise analysis: long-range dependencies require gradients to carry information across many steps, but the geometry of the loss surface makes this exponentially unlikely for plain nonlinear recurrences.

In practice, a plain RNN learns short-range patterns reliably and long-range dependencies unreliably. Exploding gradients can be patched by clipping the gradient norm before the update. Vanishing gradients are the harder problem: you cannot amplify a signal that has already decayed to nothing. This is where the LSTM intervenes.

The LSTM: a gated cell state

Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) introduced the Long Short-Term Memory cell specifically to address vanishing gradients. The key insight is to give the network a separate cell state \(C_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) that is updated additively rather than through a squashing nonlinearity. Addition, unlike repeated multiplication by a saturating sigmoid, does not shrink a gradient. Hochreiter called this the constant error carousel: a signal can ride the additive highway for many steps without decaying. The move is analogous to residual connections in deep feedforward networks — the same trick of addition over multiplication, applied in the time direction rather than the depth direction.

Three sigmoid gates, each a learned linear function of the concatenation \([h_{t-1}; x_t]\) followed by a logistic sigmoid \(\sigma\), control what the cell retains, writes, and reads:

  • The forget gate \(f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_f) \in (0,1)^{d_h}\) element-multiplies \(C_{t-1}\), deciding what fraction of each memory dimension to keep: \(f_t \approx 0\) erases, \(f_t \approx 1\) preserves.
  • The input gate \(i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_i)\) and a candidate update \(\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_c)\) together write new content: the term \(i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t\) is added to the (possibly erased) cell state.
  • The output gate \(o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}; x_t] + b_o)\) reads from the updated cell to produce the hidden state: \(h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t)\).

Putting the cell update and the readout together:

\[ C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t \] \[ h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t) \]

The \(\odot\) symbol denotes element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication. The additive structure of the \(C_t\) update is what matters for gradients: \(\partial C_t / \partial C_{t-1} = f_t\), which the network learns to hold near one when long-range information must be preserved, giving gradients an unattenuated path back through time.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014) is a streamlined variant: it merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate and eliminates the separate cell state, yielding a two-gate cell that is cheaper to compute and performs comparably to the LSTM on moderate sequence lengths.

Seq2seq and the fixed-vector bottleneck

With LSTMs as building blocks, Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (2014) — and independently Cho et al. (2014) — introduced the encoder–decoder (seq2seq) architecture for tasks that map one sequence to another, such as machine translation and summarization. An encoder LSTM reads the entire source sequence and compresses it into a single fixed-length vector — the final hidden state \(h_T \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\). A decoder LSTM is then initialized with that vector and generates the target sequence token by token, conditioning each step on the same fixed vector plus whatever the decoder has generated so far.

This works, and it was a significant step forward. But the fixed-length bottleneck is exactly what the name implies: every word the decoder will ever need to consult — every cross-lingual correspondence, every long-distance agreement — must be packed into one vector of width \(d_h\). For short sentences this is manageable. For longer ones, quality degrades measurably as the source length increases, which is visible in the empirical results of Sutskever et al. The encoder has no principled way to decide which information to prioritize when compressing, and the decoder has no way to revisit specific source positions. The alignment and attention node is the direct fix: rather than compressing the source into one vector, keep all of the encoder’s hidden states and let the decoder learn a soft, dynamic pointer back to whichever source positions it currently needs.

Problem 2 — inherent sequentiality

Even if the vanishing-gradient problem were fully solved, a second structural difficulty would remain. Because \(h_t\) depends on \(h_{t-1}\), each step of the forward pass must wait for the previous one to complete. On a sequence of length \(n\), the recurrence requires \(n\) sequential operations, regardless of how many parallel processors you have. You can parallelize across the batch dimension and across the hidden-state dimension, but you cannot parallelize across time. As models grew larger and datasets grew longer through 2015–2017, this sequential bottleneck became the primary obstacle to scaling. A GPU is a massively parallel matrix-multiply engine; feeding it one-step-at-a-time recurrences leaves most of its capacity unused.

This is arguably the more consequential of the two problems, because it is a hard ceiling on training throughput — not a matter of gradient decay that better initialization or gating might mitigate, but a dependency structure that must be broken from the outside.

Where it leads

The LSTM was not superseded because it failed to learn; it was superseded because what came after solved both problems simultaneously. The next node, alignment and attention, traces the specific path from the seq2seq fixed-vector bottleneck to Bahdanau’s soft alignment mechanism — the idea of keeping all encoder hidden states and learning to weight them dynamically. That move eliminates the bottleneck and shortens the gradient path from any decoder position to any encoder position. The transformer later takes the same idea further, replacing the sequential recurrence entirely with a parallel operation in which every position reaches every other in a single step. That is what finally breaks the sequentiality ceiling and makes training on very long sequences practical.

diagrams.caption: An RNN unrolled across time: the same weight matrices W_x and W_h apply at every step, chaining hidden states h_1 through h_T left to right. A long dashed red arrow beneath shows the gradient path back through T steps — which shrinks or explodes.
diagrams.altText: Left-to-right diagram. Input boxes x_1, x_2, x_3, ellipsis, x_T sit at the bottom. Above each, a blue hidden-state box h_1 through h_T. Blue recurrent arrows labeled W_h connect each h box to the next. Black upward arrows labeled W_x connect each x to its h. Green upward arrows lead from each h to output boxes y_1 through y_T at the top. A long red dashed arrow curves below the entire chain from h_T back to h_1 and is labeled: gradient path through T steps — shrinks or explodes.
diagrams.prompt: Structural left-to-right diagram of an RNN unrolled across time. Show four time steps explicitly: inputs x_1, x_2, x_3, then an ellipsis, then x_T, each as a labeled box at the bottom. Directly above each input box sits a hidden-state box labeled h_1, h_2, h_3, h_T. A vertical arrow labeled W_x connects each x_t up into its h_t. Horizontal arrows labeled W_h connect h_1 to h_2, h_2 to h_3, and so on through the ellipsis to h_T — these are the recurrent arrows carrying the sequential dependency. Above each h box, a vertical arrow leads to an output box y_1, y_2, y_3, y_T. On the right, add a short annotation noting that W_x and W_h are the same matrices at every step. Below the whole chain, draw a long curved dashed arrow running from h_T back to h_1, labeled: gradient path through T steps — shrinks or explodes (vanishing / exploding gradients). This bottom arrow is the visual emphasis: it shows why long-range learning is hard. Structural diagram; label every box and arrow.

diagrams.caption: Inside an LSTM cell: the cell state C_t runs as an additive highway across the top, protected by a forget gate (⊙ erase) and extended by an input gate (⊕ write). Three sigmoid gates and one tanh candidate, all fed by [h_{t-1}; x_t], control writing, retaining, and reading. The output gate produces h_t.
diagrams.altText: LSTM cell diagram. At top, a horizontal highway line from C_{t-1} on the left to C_t on the right, with two operation circles on it: a multiply circle for the forget gate and an add circle for the input gate. Below, boxes for h_{t-1} and x_t on the left feed a bus that fans out to four operations: a red sigmoid box for the forget gate f_t (arrows up to the multiply circle on the highway), a blue sigmoid box for the input gate i_t and a blue tanh box for the candidate c-tilde (their product feeds the add circle on the highway), and a green sigmoid box for the output gate o_t. On the right, a green tanh box reads from C_t, the output gate multiplies the result, and h_t emerges. A bottom note reads: cell state C_t updated additively — the constant error carousel.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram of a single LSTM cell. Layout: a thick horizontal line labeled C_{t-1} enters from the left and exits as C_t on the right — this is the cell-state highway at the top of the diagram. On the highway place two operation circles: first a multiply circle (⊙) where the forget gate is applied, then an add circle (⊕) where new information is written. Below the highway, on the left, two input boxes: h_{t-1} (previous hidden state) and x_t (current input). They join into a single bus [h,x] that fans out to four operations arranged left to right: (1) a sigmoid box labeled 'forget gate f_t' — its output arrow runs up to the multiply circle on the highway, annotated 'erase old memory?'; (2) a sigmoid box labeled 'input gate i_t' and a tanh box labeled 'candidate c-tilde' — their element-wise product feeds an upward arrow to the add circle on the highway, annotated 'write new info'; (3) a sigmoid box labeled 'output gate o_t' on the right. At the far right: a tanh box reads from C_t on the highway, the output gate multiplies the result (element-wise ⊙), producing h_t. Add a bottom caption note reading: 'Cell state C_t updated additively — the constant error carousel that lets gradients flow across many steps without vanishing.' Label every box, circle, and arrow. Structural diagram: precision over decoration.

bibliography.citation: Hochreiter, S., & Schmidhuber, J. (1997). Long Short-Term Memory. Neural Computation, 9(8), 1735–1780.
bibliography.annotation: The original LSTM paper. §1–2 motivate the vanishing-gradient problem from first principles via the constant-error-flow argument; §3 gives the gated cell equations with full derivation. Dense but precise — skim §1–2 for the gradient analysis, §3 for the gate definitions.

bibliography.citation: Sutskever, I., Vinyals, O., & Le, Q. V. (2014). Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks. NeurIPS. arXiv:1409.3215.
bibliography.annotation: Introduces the encoder–decoder (seq2seq) architecture with LSTMs. §2 specifies the fixed-vector compression; Fig. 3 shows the empirical performance drop on long sentences — the clearest signature of the bottleneck that attention later fixes.

bibliography.citation: Bengio, Y., Simard, P., & Frasconi, P. (1994). Learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is difficult. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 5(2), 157–166.
bibliography.annotation: The foundational analysis of vanishing/exploding gradients in recurrent nets. Theorem 1 (§3) gives the formal conditions; §2 provides accessible intuition. This is the paper that defined the problem LSTM was built to solve.

bibliography.citation: Olah, C. (2015). Understanding LSTM Networks. colah.github.io.
bibliography.annotation: The clearest visual walk-through of the LSTM cell equations, with diagram-based explanations of each gate's role and the cell-state highway. Ideal for anchoring the gate equations to intuition before reading the original paper. Does not cover seq2seq or the parallelism problem.
